posts.text:
The sale is over. Is the borrower out?

In about half of states, not necessarily. A statutory right of redemption lets the borrower reclaim the property for a set time after the sale, typically by paying the bid price plus interest and fees.

The window varies by state. FindLaw says it ranges from 30 days to as high as two years. Nolo lists Maine at 90 days from the judgment, unless the borrower appeals. Tennessee lists two years, and it may be waived in the loan documents.

Lenders can add the state redemption period to their exit timeline.

Bars compare 30 days, Maine at 90 days from judgment, and Tennessee at two years. Redeeming typically costs bid price plus interest and fees.

Its May 2026 Financial Stability Report says a large volume of CRE debt is scheduled to mature over the coming year, which raises the possibility of forced sales. Extending or modifying maturing loans has helped limit that risk, though that option may be increasingly limited.

posts.text:
A $280,000 loan on a $400,000 property starts at 70% LTV. Suppose nothing is paid for six months and the 11% interest is capitalized monthly.

Capitalized interest is unpaid interest added to the loan's principal balance. Each month, interest then accrues on the larger balance.

Illustrative: month one adds $2,567, so the balance is $282,567. By month six it is $295,757 and LTV is 73.9%, assuming the value stays at $400,000. The equity cushion shrinks from $120,000 to $104,243 with no new money advanced.

Lenders can check LTV on the current balance, not only the original loan amount.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Seven bars show a $280,000 loan balance growing each month as 11 percent interest is capitalized, reaching $295,757 at month six. LTV rises from 70.0% to 73.9% on a $400,000 value, and the equity cushion falls from $120,000 to $104,243. Illustrative.

posts.text:
A foreclosure sale does not always bring in enough to cover the loan. What happens to the gap?

That gap is the deficiency: the mortgage debt minus the foreclosure sale price. A deficiency judgment is a money judgment against the borrower for that difference.

Whether a lender can pursue it, and how, varies by state. In a judicial foreclosure, the lender can usually request it in the foreclosure lawsuit. After a nonjudicial foreclosure, the lender must sue separately. Some states prohibit or limit it.

Lenders can check state rules early, since they affect what recovery is possible.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Graphic titled When a foreclosure sale falls short of the debt. A formula shows debt owed minus sale price equals the deficiency. Three cards note that judicial foreclosures can include the request, nonjudicial ones need a separate suit, and some states prohibit or limit it.

sources.title: Deficiency Judgments (Anti-Deficiency Laws)
sources.quote: A "deficiency judgment" is a money judgment against a borrower for the difference between the total amount of the mortgage debt and the foreclosure sale price. As you can see, deficiency judgment laws vary widely from state to state and can be complex. In judicial foreclosures, the bank can usually request the judgment as part of the foreclosure lawsuit. With a nonjudicial foreclosure, the bank must sue the borrower following the foreclosure to get a deficiency judgment. These laws prohibit foreclosing banks from suing borrowers for deficiency judgments. Many states that allow banks to seek deficiency judgments limit the amount that banks can recover.

sources.title: Deficiency Judgments
sources.quote: The ability of a lender to seek a deficiency judgment is determined by the laws of the state where the property is situated. Some jurisdictions have rules that prevent or limit a lender's ability to pursue a deficiency judgment.

posts.text:
How big should a rehab contingency line be?

Sources give a wide range. MCAP, a Canadian lender, says a contingency can run 3% to 10% of construction costs. Kiavi says to consider at least 10-15% of the renovation budget. Your lender's terms may differ.

Illustrative: $188,000 purchase, $66,000 hard costs, loan of 90% of purchase plus the full budget.

At 8%: $5,280 contingency, $71,280 budget, $240,480 loan.

At 12%: $7,920 contingency, $73,920 budget, $243,120 loan.

The loan rises $2,640, while loan to cost barely moves (92.7% to 92.8%). Size the line on purpose.

posts.text:
An individual signs for themselves. An LLC cannot sign anything on its own, so a person signs for it. How does a lender know that person had the authority?

One law firm puts it this way: "Articles establish existence; Operating Agreements establish authority."

Lenders can ask for the articles of organization, a good standing certificate, the operating agreement, and a resolution naming the loan and the signer. Lenders can also ask for a personal guaranty, which can make the owner liable alongside the LLC.

What is required varies by state and by lender. Not legal advice.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Comparison table of lending to an individual versus an LLC. For an LLC, a person signs for the entity, so lenders can ask for articles, a good standing certificate, an operating agreement and a resolution naming the loan and signer. A personal guaranty can add the owner as a second obligor. A signature is evidence, not proof of authority.

posts.text:
Three loans, three rates. What is the portfolio yield?

Illustrative: $205,000 at 9.5%, $415,000 at 11.25%, $435,000 at 12.5%.

A simple average of the rates is 11.08%. A weighted average counts each rate in proportion to its balance. Annual interest is $19,475 + $46,687.50 + $54,375 = $120,537.50, and $120,537.50 / $1,055,000 = 11.43%.

The simple average understates the yield because the biggest balance carries the highest rate. FINRA describes a mortgage pool's coupon as a weighted average of its mortgages' rates.

Takeaway: when balances differ, weight each rate by its balance.

posts.text:
A lender records a mortgage and assumes everything is covered. A mortgage is a real property document, and the UCC generally excludes liens on real property from secured transactions rules.

Equipment is personal property. So is a borrower entity membership interest, commonly treated as a general intangible. A UCC financing statement is the usual filing to perfect many personal property interests.

Goods attached to land may be fixtures. A fixture filing is recorded where mortgages are recorded. It does not perfect interests in non-fixture goods.

Lenders can search both. Filing offices depend on the collateral and state.
posts.alt: Comparison graphic. A mortgage covers real property, the land and building, and is filed in county land records. A UCC financing statement covers personal property such as equipment and membership interests, in a separate UCC filing office. Fixture filings go where mortgages are recorded. Search both.

posts.text:
Can an HOA lien come ahead of a first mortgage?

In some states, part of it can. Nolo describes a super lien as the portion of an HOA lien given higher priority than even a first-mortgage holder. In Colorado, six months of assessments get that status. In Nevada, it is nine months.

Foreclosing a super lien may eliminate the first mortgage. Rules and amounts vary by state.

Lenders can ask in diligence whether the property sits in an HOA, whether assessments are current, and whether state law gives HOAs a super lien.

posts.text:
What does a $750,000 loan earn on the lender's own money when a credit line funds part of it?

A warehouse line is short-term, revolving borrowing that mortgage lenders use to fund loans before selling them. Say a lender uses a similar line. Terms vary by lender.

The loan earns 10.75 percent, or $80,625 a year. The line funds 65 percent, $487,500, at 7.75 percent, costing $37,781.25. The spread is $42,843.75 on $262,500 of the lender's own money, or 16.32 percent.

That ignores fees and losses. Compare line cost to loan yield first.

posts.text:
The tenants keep paying rent on a building in foreclosure. Who collects it?

A lender can ask the court to appoint a receiver. A receiver is an unbiased third party who protects the property from damage and lost rental income. Depending on the order, the receiver may collect rents, operate the property and arrange repairs. The receiver generally does not take title.

Courts may look at whether the borrower turned over rents and whether the property is maintained. Timing and standards vary by state and by the loan documents.

Lenders can ask counsel early whether a receiver fits the loan.

posts.text:
You rehabbed a property and the appraisal came in well above what you paid. Will the exit lender count it?

That depends on seasoning: how long you must own a property before a lender refinances against its current appraised value. Inside the window, many lenders lend against the lower of the appraised value and the purchase price.

Fannie Mae generally requires six months on title for a cash-out refinance, with exceptions. A number of DSCR lenders use current value after three to six months. Rules vary by lender.

Ask early what seasoning the exit lender requires.

posts.text:
A lender advertises 10.2 percent on a $2,200,000 portfolio. Then one loan loses $44,000. What is the yield now?

Here, net yield means interest earned minus losses, divided by the amount lent.

Gross: $2,200,000 times 10.2 percent is $224,400 of interest.

Net: $224,400 minus $44,000 is $180,400. Divided by $2,200,000, that is 8.2 percent.

The loss equals 2.0 percent of the portfolio, so it took 2.0 points off the yield.

Takeaway: a gross rate shows what borrowers owe on paper. Net yield shows what the lender kept.

posts.text:
A lender asks for a Phase I. What does that report cover?

A Phase I environmental site assessment reviews site records, includes a site visit, and interviews people who know the property. It does not include lab testing of samples.

It looks for a recognized environmental condition: the presence or likely presence of hazardous substances or petroleum products at the property.

EPA recognizes ASTM E1527-21 as one standard for buyers seeking liability protection, with work updated within one year, and key parts within 180 days, before acquisition.

Lenders can ask which standard and timing they want.

posts.text:
A draw request says the work is done. Photos are how a lender can see it.

Jobsite photo guides suggest photos that hold up on their own, and lenders can ask for them:

Dated and geotagged, so the record is traceable.

A wide shot first, then close-ups of the detail.

The same spot and angle each time, so progress is obvious.

In focus, clearly showing the item. Blurry or small photos may mean an inspector is asked to return to the property.

What a lender accepts varies by lender, so confirm it before the borrower submits.

posts.text:
What does asset-based lending mean?

It means the loan is secured by collateral, with the focus on the collateral. One law firm says the focus is on the collateral and not primarily on the borrower.

Conventional lenders, the same firm says, are more concerned with credit record, income, balance sheet, and cash flow. For consumer loans secured by a home, federal rules require a good faith ability-to-repay determination that considers income or assets other than the home. Business purpose loans are outside that rule.

Takeaway: with asset-based loans, the property carries the file. Rules vary by state.

Conventional lending: the borrower's credit record, income, balance sheet and cash flow. A note adds that the federal consumer ability-to-repay rule looks at income or assets other than the home.

posts.text:
A $355,000 loan closes with 2.5 points. Does the lender keep all of them?

Points are a percentage of the loan amount charged for originating it. Here, 2.5 points is $8,875. If 1 point goes to a broker, that is $3,550, leaving the lender $5,325.

Add 12 months of interest-only at 10.3 percent, $36,565, and the lender collects $41,890. That is an 11.8 percent yield. Keep all 2.5 points and it is $45,440, or 12.8 percent.

Broker fees can be built into points. It varies by lender. Compare yields on the points you actually keep. Numbers illustrative.

posts.alt: Stacked bar splitting 2.5 points ($8,875) on an illustrative $355,000 loan: 1 point ($3,550) to a broker and 1.5 points ($5,325) kept by the lender. Two cards: 11.8 percent lender yield with the broker share, 12.8 percent keeping all points, at 10.3 percent interest-only for 12 months.

posts.text:
Lending on a conversion or a multi-unit building? Zoning is the first gate for whether a plan is allowed.

Lenders can run a short check:

1. Get the zoning district in writing. Some cities issue a zoning verification letter.

2. Ask whether the planned use is permitted, not only the district.

3. Ask whether the current use is legal nonconforming. That status can be lost after abandonment or destruction.

4. Ask about code violations separately. Some cities handle Fire Code requests apart from the zoning letter.

What a letter covers varies by city. Not legal advice.

posts.text:
What makes a loan a portfolio loan?

The lender keeps it on its own books instead of selling it in the secondary market.

That choice changes the lender's options. Lenders get to set the loan terms and documentation requirements on portfolio loans, which allows some flexibility. It also means taking on more risk when credit and underwriting criteria are loosened.

It changes cash, too. A lender that sells a loan can use the proceeds to fund additional mortgages. Holding a loan keeps that capital tied up.

Holding keeps control of the terms.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two comparison cards. A sold loan is held by the buyer and the lender receives sale proceeds that can fund additional mortgages. A portfolio loan stays on the lender's books as an investment asset, with the lender free to set terms and taking on more risk.

sources.quote: Portfolio loans are loans the lender keeps on its own books and does not sell. The lender, meanwhile, can use the proceeds from selling the loan to fund additional mortgages.

sources.quote: A portfolio loan is a type of mortgage a lender keeps instead of selling in the secondary market. Lenders get to set the loan terms and documentation requirements on portfolio loans, allowing for some flexibility. Lenders take on more risk when they loosen credit and underwriting criteria

posts.text:
A $325,000 loan closes on November 19. How much interest covers the odd days before the first full month?

Illustrative, at 10 percent: the 19th through the 30th is 12 days. Actual/360 counts real days over a 360-day year, so $325,000 x 10 percent / 360 is about $90.28 a day, or $1,083.33 for the stub.

Day count matters again later. In a 31-day month, actual/360 charges 31 days, $2,798.61. A 30/360 note treats every month as 30 days: $2,708.33.

Lenders can confirm the day count and start date in the note. These vary by lender.

posts.text:
Vacant or tenanted? The same collateral can follow two different paths after foreclosure.

Vacant: there is no tenant lease to work around.

Tenanted: one law firm notes a foreclosed property must often be sold subject to the remaining lease term. In residential foreclosures, federal law requires a new owner to give a bona fide tenant 90 days notice before eviction. A commercial lease may even rank ahead of the mortgage.

Lenders can review the lease term, rent, deposits and subordination language, and ask for an estoppel. Rules vary by state. Not legal advice.
